items.title: 13.8.1 Reactions of halides with aqueous silver ion

source_refs.note: Topic 13.8.1 with Figure 13.2, printed pages 297-298. The printed general equation ('Ag- ... 2AgX') is written correctly and noted.

blocks.text: Insoluble silver halides form when halide ions react with aqueous silver nitrate, X-(aq) + Ag+(aq) gives AgX(s); the reactions are used in qualitative analysis to identify halide ions and are called the silver nitrate test. No reaction is visible with fluoride, because silver fluoride is soluble in water. Silver and chloride ions give a white precipitate of silver chloride, soluble in dilute ammonia: Ag+ + Cl- gives AgCl(s). Silver and bromide ions give a cream-coloured precipitate of silver bromide, sparingly soluble in concentrated ammonia: Ag+ + Br- gives AgBr(s). Silver and iodide ions give a yellow precipitate of silver iodide, insoluble in ammonia: Ag+ + I- gives AgI(s) (Figure 13.2).

blocks.alt: Top left: four test tubes for fluoride, chloride, bromide and iodide with no precipitate, a white, a cream and a yellow precipitate, with the ammonia result under each and the equations. Top right: the cold and hot sodium hydroxide reactions of chlorine with the oxidation states of chlorine in each product. Bottom: the hydrolysis of chlorine in water, how HOCl and OCl- disinfect, and the pH, dose and contact-time factors with a pH bar.
blocks.caption: The silver nitrate test with ammonia, chlorine with cold and hot sodium hydroxide, and chlorination of water (original diagram after Figure 13.2, Table 13.6 and topics 13.8 to 13.11).
blocks.long_description: Silver ions precipitate chloride as white silver chloride, bromide as cream silver bromide and iodide as yellow silver iodide, while fluoride stays in solution; ammonia then dissolves the chloride in dilute solution and the bromide only in concentrated solution, and leaves the iodide untouched, which identifies each ion. Chlorine disproportionates in alkali: with cold dilute sodium hydroxide it gives chloride and chlorate(I), with hot concentrated alkali chloride and chlorate(V), the same element being oxidised and reduced at once. In water chlorine hydrolyses to hydrochloric and chloric(I) acids; the neutral HOCl molecule penetrates bacterial cell walls and oxidises their proteins, enzymes and nucleic acids, so chlorination at a pH between 6 and 7.5, with enough dose and contact time, disinfects drinking water cheaply.

blocks.prompt: Why does aqueous fluoride give no precipitate with silver nitrate when the other halides do?
blocks.explanation: Silver fluoride is soluble in water, unlike the chloride, bromide and iodide of silver, whose solubility products are tiny and fall from chloride to iodide. So Ag+ and F- stay in solution and nothing is seen.

items: Ag+ + X- gives AgX(s): F- none (AgF soluble); Cl- white; Br- cream; I- yellow. The silver nitrate test identifies halides in qualitative analysis.
